## Use standard written prose

### Say things clearly

#### Do not leave out the subject

Avoid:

> ❌ After clicking the save button, the changes are saved to the database.

Prefer:

> ✅ After **the user** clicks the save button, **the system** saves the changes to the database.

#### Do not leave out the predicate

Avoid:

> ❌ This project is named MyProj. A personal side project, maintained by one developer.

Prefer:

> ✅ This project is named MyProj. **It is** a personal side project, maintained by one developer.

#### Make references explicit

Avoid:

> ❌ The server receives the request and hands it to the backend; the backend processes it and returns it to the frontend.

Prefer:

> ✅ The server receives the request and hands **the request** to the backend; the backend processes **that request** and returns **the result** to the frontend.

Name the referent. The reader should not have to scroll back to work out what **it** points to. Even when a pronoun is unambiguous, piling them up still costs the reader effort.

#### State what a qualifier applies to

Examples:

1.  Avoid:

    > ❌ After the concurrency limit was raised, response time grew noticeably. The bottleneck is probably the connection pool running out, so raise the limit first and see.

    Which limit is meant?

    Prefer:

    > ✅ After the concurrency limit was raised, response time grew noticeably. The bottleneck is probably the **database connection pool** running out, so raise **the pool’s** limit first and see.

2.  Avoid:

    > ❌ The attack work is driven by the model, and **the next command** cannot be reviewed in advance.

    “The next command” appears out of nowhere, and the reader cannot tell what it refers to.

    Prefer:

    > ✅ The attack work is driven by the model: attack commands are generated by the model on the spot, the next command does not exist beforehand, and therefore it cannot be reviewed in advance.

#### Say who acts and who receives

With words such as reply, forward, hand over, or return, state who gives what to whom.

#### Do not use opaque abbreviations or codes

Avoid:

> ❌ MyProj won first prize in a certain competition (1/114514).

Prefer:

> ✅ MyProj won first prize in a certain competition, ranking first among 114514 entries.

### Choose words carefully

#### Avoid invented abstract jargon

Avoid:

> ❌ This module handles the birth and death of containers.

Prefer:

> ✅ This module manages **the creation and destruction** of containers.

### Avoid over-colloquial prose

Use written prose in the body of a document. Keep the tone of a casual conversation out of it.

Avoid:

> ❌ This thing shoves the data into the database.

Prefer:

> ✅ This component writes the data to the database.

### Do not negate out of nowhere

Start with the examples:

Q: What color is the box?

Avoid:

> ❌ It is **not** red, **not** green, but blue.

Prefer:

> ✅ It is blue.

When you describe something, say what it is. If nobody brought up a thing, do not deny that thing out of nowhere; do not write “it is not xxx but yyy”.

Use a denial only to clear up a real misunderstanding. Do not invent something merely in order to deny it.

The test: the reading you deny must already have come up, or must genuinely invite confusion.

Examples:

1.  > - Q: That box looks red to me. Is it the red one?
    > - ✅ A: It is not the red one. This box is blue.

2.  > - Q: What is a soft delete?
    > - ✅ A: A soft delete marks a record as deleted without physically removing it. ✅ State what it is first, then deny the reading that invites confusion.
    > - ❌ A: A soft delete does not physically remove the record; it marks the record as deleted. ❌ The question asked what it is, so answer that first.

### Do not use em dashes

Split the sentence in two, or use a colon or a comma instead.

### Do not use quotes or parentheses to smuggle in explanations

If a fact belongs in the text, state it in the text.

## Prose flow

### Keep the logic connected and use transitions

- Make the cause, order, and contrast between sentences and paragraphs explicit. Do not leave the reader to infer them.
- Point the relation out with connectives such as “first … then …”, “if … then …”, “therefore”, or “on the other hand”.

Avoid:

> ❌ The server receives the request. If the cache has it, return it. If not, query the database. If the database does not have it either, return 404.

Prefer:

> ✅ When the server receives the request, it checks the cache first. **If** the cache has the entry, **then** it returns the cached result; **if** the cache misses, **then** it queries the database; **if** the database does not have the entry either, **then** it returns 404.

### State the through-line, the topic, and the purpose

The article has to hold together logically and connect naturally. Every part should serve the through-line and relate to the purpose and the topic. Do not write down whatever comes to mind. Do not leave the reader wondering: “I was reading about xxx, and now I am reading about yyy. What does yyy have to do with xxx?”

A common failure is putting related material in the wrong place: the opening promises one through-line, the middle spreads out general background, and neither the way into it nor the way out of it is explained, so the reader gets lost there.

Avoid:

> ❌ This article follows one web request: from the moment you press Enter to the moment the page appears in front of you. You type `example.com` into the address bar and press Enter. The browser does not know which server that name maps to, so the first thing it does is look up the address.
>
> DNS was born in 1983 to replace hand-maintained host tables. DNS is hierarchical: the root domain, the top-level domains, and the authoritative domains delegate downward, level by level. There are two kinds of query: a recursive query hands the whole question to a server to handle; an iterative query asks its way down the hierarchy and assembles the answer itself. Record types vary as well: A records, CNAME records, and MX records each have their uses.
>
> Once the address is known, the browser opens a connection to the server.

A reader who reaches the middle will ask: “I was following this one request, and now I am reading a general introduction to DNS. What does any of this have to do with this request?”

Prefer:

> ✅ This article follows one web request: from the moment you press Enter to the moment the page appears in front of you. You type `example.com` into the address bar and press Enter. The browser does not know where the server for `example.com` is, so the first thing it does is look up the address, and this step is called name resolution. The browser checks its own cache first; if the cache does not have the name, it hands the name to the local DNS server. The local server does not know either, so it asks upward level by level until some server gives an answer. With the address in hand, the browser opens a connection to the server.

The DNS material is still there, but the sentence “the browser does not know where the server is” brings it in, only the part this request needs is told, and “with the address in hand” hands the reader back to the through-line.

## Back every rule with examples

Example:

> Q: How do you sum an arithmetic series?

Avoid:

> ❌ A: Add the first term to the last term, multiply by the number of terms, and divide by 2.

Prefer:

> ✅ A: Add the first term to the last term, multiply by the number of terms, and divide by 2. **For example**, take the series 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Its first term is 2, its last term is 10, and it has 5 terms, so its sum is `(2+10)*5/2=30`.

## Analogy and metaphor

- Use them only at the right moment. Do not overuse them.
- An overused or poorly chosen metaphor raises the cost of understanding and lowers the depth.
- The analogy has to fit. Prefer an analogy drawn from the same domain, and use abstract metaphors sparingly.

Avoid:

> ❌ Garbage collection is like a diligent cleaner who sweeps the floor every day.

Prefer:

> ✅ The `Task` type in C# is the counterpart of JavaScript’s `Promise`. ✅ an analogy from the same domain

## Layout

Beyond making the content easy to understand, work on the layout so that it reads comfortably.

### Break up lines and paragraphs

Break a paragraph where the topic changes. Do not string small clauses together all the way to the end.

Avoid:

> ❌ A cache reduces the load on the database. When reading data, check the cache first; on a hit, return the value; on a miss, query the database and write the result back to the cache. A cache has costs too. It takes memory, and its data can go stale, so you have to set an expiry policy, otherwise you will read old values.

Prefer:

> ✅ A cache reduces the load on the database. When reading data, check the cache first; if it hits, return the value at once; if it misses, query the database and write the result back to the cache.
>
> A cache has costs too. It takes memory, and its data can go stale, so you have to set an expiry policy, otherwise you will read old values.

### Use lists and bold text

Lists, bold text, and similar devices give the article more structure.

Avoid:

> ❌ First, xxx; second, yyy

Prefer:

> ✅
>
> 1.  xxx
> 2.  yyy

### Make quotations explicit and prominent

Avoid:

- ❌ The snapshot says roughly this: project name: “juice-shop”; attackers running: zero; concurrency limit: seven; attacker prompts available: exactly one, named tsinswreng-security. All the model can see is the text sent to it; what the system stores internally, the model knows nothing about.

Prefer:

- ✅ The snapshot says roughly this:

  > - project name: “juice-shop”;
  > - attackers running: 0;
  > - concurrency limit: 7;
  > - attacker prompts available: exactly one, named tsinswreng-security

  All the model can see is the text sent to it; what the system stores internally, the model knows nothing about.

Note: in Typst, a block quotation uses this syntax:

```
#quote(block:true)[
  quoted text
]
```

## Comprehensive examples

1.  Avoid:

    > ❌ This workspace is MyProj. A multi-agent collaboration platform for a certain scenario, built as a Bun monorepo. First prize in a certain competition (1/114514). **A company project with two repositories**: on the open-source side, `company-org/MyProj` on GitHub (a company org); on the internal side, `ComMyProj` (hosted on the company GitLab rather than GitHub, with a history completely independent of the open-source side, and the latest changes all living there; the user is a company employee who took over development). **Main development ground (from 2026-09-18)**: the `dev` branch of `ComMyProj` in this workspace.

    Prefer:

    > ✅ This workspace belongs to the MyProj project. MyProj is a multi-agent collaboration platform for a certain scenario, laid out as a single Bun repository. MyProj won first prize in a certain competition, ranking first among 114514 entries.
    >
    > MyProj is a company project with two remote repositories:
    >
    > - the open-source repository on GitHub, named `company-org/MyProj` and owned by the company org;
    > - the internal repository, named `ComMyProj`, hosted on the company GitLab. It shares no commit history with the open-source side on GitHub. The user is a company employee who took over development.
    >
    > The latest changes live in the internal repository, so since 2026-09-18 the main development ground has been the `dev` branch of `ComMyProj` in this workspace.

2.  Avoid:

    > ❌ When starting a container, the task brief goes in along with the startup command. After that, every step inside the container streams back to the host over rpc in real time. Why split it into these two layers: the hands-on work is model-driven, the next command cannot be reviewed in advance, it cannot be allowed to run directly on the host; one attacker per container, whoever breaks the environment does not drag in the others or the host; the environment is one-shot, whatever was installed and whatever junk was left all disappear with the container.

    Prefer:

    > ✅ When a container starts, the task brief is sent into the container along with the startup command. After that, every step inside the container streams back to the host over rpc in real time. Why the work is split into a host process and a container: the attack work is driven by the model, attack commands are generated by the model on the spot, and the next command the model emits cannot be reviewed in advance, so such a command cannot run directly on the host. One attacker gets one container. Even if the environment in one container breaks, it does not drag in the other containers or the host. The environment is one-shot: whatever was installed in the container and whatever junk was left disappears together with the container.

3.  Avoid:

    > ❌ Dispatch decisions only land once they reach `runtime`: build the image, start the container, recycle the container. One attacker per container, one isolated sandbox per task: breaking one does not affect another, the environment is thrown away once used. When the container starts, the host assembles the task brief and sends it in along with the startup command. The brief is a template with five parts: the project name and description; the list of target entry points, each with a fingerprint; two boards from the intelligence pool plus three-paragraph summaries of the reports already turned in; the list of behaviour requirements; and finally the kickoff note, attached at the end as “follow with the highest priority”.

    Prefer:

    > ✅ Dispatch decisions are carried out by `runtime`, which does three things: build the image, create the container, and recycle the container. One attacker gets one container, and one task is one isolated sandbox: damage to one container’s environment does not affect the others, and the environment is discarded together with the container when the task ends. When a container starts, the host sends the assembled task brief into it along with the startup command. The brief is a template made up of five parts:
    >
    > 1.  the project name and description
    > 2.  the list of target entry points, each with a fingerprint
    > 3.  two boards from the intelligence pool and three-paragraph summaries of the reports already turned in
    > 4.  the list of behaviour requirements
    > 5.  the kickoff note, attached at the end of the brief and marked as the highest priority

## Rewriting

Rewriting means turning text that has problems into text that reads clearly.

Points to work through:

- Go through the rules above one by one and check each of them.
- Read the text as a human reader would: is it easy to understand? Is anything wrong with it?
- Does the rewritten text still carry the information it needs?

### Rewriting must not lose information

Rewriting only changes how something is said, so the useful information has to survive the rewrite. Only content that is genuinely redundant may be dropped.

## Self-check

Ask yourself two questions:

- Does it satisfy the rules above?
- Read as a human reader: is it easy to understand? Is anything wrong with it?
